mione1809act.heading: The act itself, read at last
mione1809act.grade: doc — Mione, Matrimoni 1809, act N. 1, read at high magnification 14 September 2026
mione1809act.lead: The allegati are the paperwork. **This is the marriage.** Act number one of the Mione register for 1809, and it settles the pairing this page had graded *inferred* — while correcting two things this archive had published about the groom.

act.when: **Monday 13 February 1809, at half past eleven in the morning**, before the Officer of the Civil State of the Comune di Mione, **Giacomo Micoli**
act.who: **«Erman de Franceschi Gio: Pietro»**, aged **fifty-six**, *agricoltore*, of Mione — **widower of the late Cattarina née Carlevaris** — son of the late **Pietro Erman** and **Maddalena née de Franceschi**
act.child: **«Orsola de Franceschi»**, aged **forty**, *villica*, of the same village — daughter of the late **Pietro de Franceschi** and **Maddalena née Fedeli**
act.brought: His birth act, read into the record: born **28 April 1752** at Mione. Hers: born **11 April 1768**, the date the baptismal extract gave.
act.witnesses: **Valentino Lupieri**, 39 · **Matteo Lupieri**, 21, his brother · **Giovanni Colledan**, 58, tailor · **Antonio Bressan**, 26, servant — *all of Luint*
act.signed: **«Gio: Pietro Erman de Franceschi — per me e per Orsola de Franceschi mia moglie che non sa scrivere.»** He signed for them both.
act.ref: Archivio di Stato di Udine · Stato civile napoleonico · Mione · Matrimoni · 1809 · segnatura 12983-series · Antenati ark an_ua667518, image 3 of 9

why.lab: Two corrections, and the better story underneath
why.text:
This archive published, hours earlier, that the groom was **«Giovanni Pietro Antonio Cramaro», born 28 April 1758**. Both halves were wrong.

His surname is **Erman**. His birth year is **1752** — the act says fifty-six in February 1809, and reads his birth act as 28 April 1752; the last digit of the year had been cropped out of the zoom used on the extract, and was guessed.

And **«cramaro» was never a surname.** The priest wrote *«figlio di Pietro cramaro del villaggio di Mione»* — Pietro **the cramar**, the Carnian pedlar who walked the passes into Austria and down into Istria. This page had called the Cramaro name «the road this family walked» and graded it as a surname. **It was the road. It was just never a name.**

why.lab: She could not write, and he wrote for her
why.text:
*«per me e per Orsola de Franceschi mia moglie che non sa scrivere.»*

Orsola was forty years old, the daughter of a household that this archive can now follow back to her grandfather **Matteo**, and she could not sign her own marriage. Her husband signed for her.

It is the same hand-to-mouth literacy the Muina papers showed the year before, where **Maria Corva** and **Galante** could not write and their children could. **Here the woman is on the wrong side of that line, and her husband on the right one.**

why.lab: Three more of the family in the same nine pages
why.text:
Reading the whole register rather than the one act found three more:

**Osvaldo de Franceschi, aged 22, *falegname***, standing witness on **9 August 1809**. This matters: the archive has flagged that «nineteen in 1806 and twenty-six in 1810 are three years apart and cannot both be right». **Twenty-two in August 1809 puts him with the nineteen** — born about 1787 — and leaves the «twenty-six» of 1810 as the odd reading.

**Francesco de Franceschi, aged 25**, witness on **21 September 1809** — born about 1784, and almost certainly the Francesco the tailor who married Margherita Gortan.

**Pasqua née de Franceschi**, named as the living mother of a bride: **Maddalena Luchini, born 23 January 1789** at Luincis, daughter of **Pietro Luchini and Pasqua nata de Franceschi**. The archive had Pasqua «married into the Luchin» as a household. **Here she is, dated, with a daughter of her own marrying.**

why.lab: What this says about method
why.text:
The allegati gave the surname. **The register gave the truth about it.** A file of loose supporting papers is written by several hands in several places and copies what it is told; the marriage act is written once, by the registrar, with both parties in front of him and the documents on the table.

**Read the allegati to find the marriage. Read the register to believe it.**

mione1806act.heading: And the 1806 register, which holds a wedding the allegati had only half-told
mione1806act.grade: doc — Mione, Matrimoni 1806, act N. 1, read 14 September 2026. The bride's stated age and the birth year read into the act differ by a year; both readings are given and neither is forced.
mione1806act.lead: The Mione marriage register opens in **August 1806** with a De Franceschi wedding — and it is the marriage whose allegato this archive read earlier today, when a first transcription of *«Giovanna, daughter of Giacomo q. Gio: Batta, born 1785»* had to be corrected on the page to **Giacoma, Osvaldo, 1789**. Here is the act that allegato belonged to.

act.when: **August 1806, at nine in the morning**, Comune di Mione, Cantone di Forni, Dipartimento di Passariano
act.who: **«Ignazio di Zuato»**, *negoziante* — a merchant — aged twenty-eight, of **Chialina**, born **13 December 1777**, son of the late **Gio: Giacomo di Zuato** and **Cattarina née Cneva**
act.child: **«Giacoma de Franceschi»**, daughter of the late **Osvaldo de Franceschi** and **Cattarina née Gobbi** — the mother's surname is new to this archive
act.brought: Her father's **written consent of 7 September 1805**, and the groom's mother's of 8 September 1805 — both parents of the couple consenting by letter a year before the wedding
act.witnesses: **Batta Brenci**, **Gio: Batta del Missier**, **Giuseppe del q. Michiel**, **Pietro Ruspil** — all four signing in their own hands
act.signed: **«Giacoma de Franceschi q.m Osualdo affermo»** — she signs her own name. The registrar is **Giovanni Micoli-Toscano**, with **Batta Micoli-Toscano** as deputy.
act.ref: Archivio di Stato di Udine · Stato civile napoleonico · Mione · Matrimoni · 1806 · Antenati ark an_ua667516, image 3 of 3

why.lab: Osvaldo the elder, bracketed to the month
why.text:
This archive has spent months with **«an older Osvaldo, dead before October 1806»** as a name with no sighting. Today has given him three.

He stood **godfather in January 1789** (the 1812 allegati). He **consented in writing to his daughter's marriage on 7 September 1805**. And by **August 1806** he is *«il fu Osvaldo»* — dead.

**Alive in September 1805, dead by August 1806.** That is a twelve-month window, from two documents, for a man who had no date at all this morning.

why.lab: She could write, and Orsola could not
why.text:
**«Giacoma de Franceschi q.m Osualdo affermo m.p.»** — *manu propria*, in her own hand.

Three years later her kinswoman **Orsola**, aged forty, could not sign her own marriage and her husband signed for her. Giacoma, at eighteen, could.

Two De Franceschi women, one village, three years apart, on opposite sides of the line. **This archive will not pretend to know why**, but it is the kind of thing that is only visible because both acts were read rather than indexed.

why.lab: A merchant, and the road again
why.text:
Giacoma married a ***negoziante*** — a merchant — of **Chialina**, the next village. Orsola married into the **Erman**, who had been in Istria in 1679. The Muina bride of 1808 married a farmer.

**The De Franceschi daughters of this valley married trade as often as land**, and trade is what took this family out of the mountains.

why.lab: The registrar is the palace
why.text:
The act is signed by **Giovanni Micoli-Toscano, Ufficiale dello Stato Civile**, with **Batta Micoli-Toscano** deputising.

The Micoli Toscano palace at Mione holds the **1679 Gorto contracts** — the ones naming the Erman who went to Istria with Zuane De Franceschi. In 1806 that same family is registering this family's marriages, and in 1794 one of them stood godfather at Nave. **They are not a lead to chase; they are the neighbours.**

mionedeaths1808.heading: A child of five, and a household nobody had
mionedeaths1808.grade: doc — Mione, Morti 1808, read at high magnification 14 September 2026
mionedeaths1808.lead: The death registers were opened next, on the reasoning that a death act states an **age**, and an age back-dates a birth into the years before civil registration began. The first one read produced a household this archive did not have — and a fact about how this family married.

act.when: **30 April 1808, at five in the afternoon**, at Mione. Registered the same day by **Valentino Lupieri**, who went to the house on being notified
act.who: **«il cadavere di Francesc'Antonio de Franceschi … nell'età d'anni cinque»** — a boy of five, so born about 1803, before any register that survives
act.child: His parents, as the witnesses declared them: **Antonio de Franceschi**, by trade **«sartore»** — a tailor — and **Giovanna, «pure de Franceschi»**, *«economa di casa»*, both living at Mione
act.brought: **«pure de Franceschi» — also a de Franceschi.** Both parents carry the surname
act.witnesses: **Gio: Pietro Erman de Franceschi**, *«dell'età d'anni cinquantacinque in circa»*, farmer — and **Agostino Brencis**, 32, carpenter
act.signed: Valentino Lupieri, Officer of the Civil State
act.ref: Archivio di Stato di Udine · Stato civile napoleonico · Mione · Morti · 1808 · Antenati ark an_ua667555, image 6 of 11

why.lab: The family married itself
why.text:
*«da Antonio de Franceschi, e da Giovanna **pure de Franceschi** giugali»* — from Antonio de Franceschi and Giovanna, **also** a de Franceschi, married.

This archive has been tracing De Franceschi daughters marrying **out** — into the Erman, the di Zuato, the Luchin. **Here is a couple where both sides are the surname**, in the same village, and the registrar thought it worth the word *pure* to make clear he had not written the name twice by mistake.

In a village of this size that is what you would expect and it is still worth recording: by 1803 there were enough De Franceschi households at Mione for two of them to marry each other.

why.lab: A fifth trade, and a second tailor
why.text:
Antonio is a **sartore**. This archive already has **Francesco de Franceschi, tailor**, married to Margherita Gortan at Mione — and has made something of it, because the tailor is the **cramar** trade that walked into Istria.

**Antonio is a second one.** Two tailors of this surname in one village in the same decade, and neither is the other: Francesco's wife is a Gortan, Antonio's is a de Franceschi.

The household is new to this archive. It joins the four from the birth registers and the fifth from 1806.

why.lab: And the 1809 groom, a year before his wedding
why.text:
The first witness is **Gio: Pietro Erman de Franceschi**, about fifty-five, a farmer of Mione. Ten months later the same man — fifty-six, farmer, of Mione — marries **Orsola de Franceschi**.

He is here in April 1808 as a **widower**, standing at a neighbour's dead child. The marriage act of 1809 records that he had buried a wife, **Cattarina née Carlevaris**. **This is the man in the year between.**

why.lab: And a month-old girl, whose birth this archive already had
why.text:
**Morti 1810, act N. 1 — 28 January 1810, eight in the evening, Mione.** The registrar **Giacomo Micoli** views the body of **«De Franceschi Anna Cecilia»**, *«in età di un mese»* — one month old.

The witnesses declare her born at Mione *«da **Francesco de Franceschi**, e **Margherita nata Gortan** jugali, di professione **sarto il primo**, agricoltrice la seconda»*. Witnesses **Antonio Bressan**, 26, servant, and **Matteo Lupieri**, 22, *possidente*, both of **Luint**.

**This archive already had her birth.** The Mione birth index for 1806–1810 *«opens on three De Franceschi entries, the first three lines of the whole book: Anna-Maria, **Anna-Cecilia** and Gio: Batta»*. Here is the other end of the shortest of those three lives — **born about December 1809, dead on 28 January 1810.**

It also confirms, from a second act, that **Francesco the tailor's wife was Margherita Gortan** — and Francesco is one of the two brothers of the act three weeks earlier.

why.lab: Why the death registers are the right place to be looking
why.text:
A marriage act gives ages for two people. A **death** act gives an age for anyone, at any age, including the people who were already old when the registers opened.

**Francesc'Antonio was born about 1803** — three years before the first Napoleonic register at Mione. He exists nowhere else. **Every death act in these nine volumes is a person reaching back before the series**, and that is where the generation of Matteo and the elder Osvaldo will be found, if they are found at all.

mionebrothers.heading: «Francesco ed Osvaldo fratelli de Franceschi»
mionebrothers.grade: doc for the brotherhood, the ages and the trades · inf for the parentage, which is argued from three other acts and not stated in this one
mionebrothers.lead: The 1809 death register opens on a neighbour's funeral, and the two men who came to identify the body are the single most useful sentence this archive has found in the Mione series. **They are named as brothers.**

act.when: **14 January 1809**, Mione. The registrar **Valentino Lupieri** viewing the body of **Maria della Vecchia**, aged thirty, wife of Giuseppe Pol, born at Mielis in the Comune di Comeglians
act.who: **«Presenti alla ricognizione furono Francesco ed Osvaldo fratelli de Franceschi»** — present at the identification were **Francesco and Osvaldo, brothers, de Franceschi**
act.witnesses: *«l'uno e l'altro di Mione, non parenti della defunta»* — both of Mione, and no relation to the dead woman. They were there as neighbours, which is why the register bothered to say how they were related **to each other**
act.signed: Both sign in their own hands: **«Francesco de Franceschi»** and **«Osvaldo Ant.o de Franceschi»**
act.ref: Archivio di Stato di Udine · Stato civile napoleonico · Mione · Morti · 1809 · act N. 1 · Antenati ark an_ua667556, image 3 of 9

why.lab: Two of the four households are one household
why.text:
This archive has carried **Francesco, a tailor, and Margherita Gortan of Mione** and **Osvaldo, a carpenter, and Cattarina Brencis of Mione** as two of the four Mione households, side by side in a table, with nothing joining them.

**They are brothers.** One sentence in a stranger's death act says so, and both men signed underneath it.

The village had fewer De Franceschi families than the register index suggested. It had **more De Franceschi brothers**.

why.lab: And probably a third sibling, and a father
why.text:
Three other acts now line up behind that sentence.

The **1806 birth act** has *«Osvaldo de Franceschi, son of the late Osvaldo»*, about nineteen. The **1806 marriage act** has **Giacoma de Franceschi, «q.m Osualdo»**, daughter of the late **Osvaldo** and **Cattarina née Gobbi**. And the elder Osvaldo consented to that marriage in writing on 7 September 1805 and was dead by August 1806.

**If the Osvaldo of 1806 is the Osvaldo of 1809 — and the ages agree — then Francesco, Osvaldo Antonio and Giacoma are three children of the elder Osvaldo and Cattarina née Gobbi.** The four households of the birth registers collapse toward **one family with a dead father**.

**This is inference, and it is labelled as such.** No document says the three are siblings of each other. What the documents say is that two of them are brothers, that two of them had a dead father called Osvaldo, and that all of it happens in one small village inside three years.

why.lab: What the ages are worth, and what they are not
why.text:
Osvaldo's declared age now exists four times: **nineteen** in October 1806, **twenty-two** in January 1809, **twenty-two** in August 1809, and **twenty-six** in 1810.

Three of the four agree on a birth around **1786–87**. The fourth does not, and this page has already noted that «nineteen in 1806 and twenty-six in 1810 cannot both be right».

**They still cannot. But it is now three against one**, and the odd reading is the 1810 one. Declared ages in these acts are what a neighbour said on a doorstep, not what a register held — and this is a clean demonstration of how far they can drift.

why.lab: Both brothers could write
why.text:
**«Francesco de Franceschi»** and **«Osvaldo Ant.o de Franceschi»**, in their own hands, at the foot of the act.

A tailor and a carpenter, twenty-four and twenty-two, in a mountain village in 1809, both signing. Their kinswoman **Orsola**, forty years old, could not sign her own marriage six weeks later and her husband signed for her.

**The literacy in this family is not a line drawn by generation. It is drawn by sex**, and this archive should stop being surprised by it.

mionepaolo.heading: Anna, wife of Paolo, dead at forty-four — and the table that found her
mionepaolo.grade: doc for the act · the reading of «jeri» for the day of death is the one word in it I would not stake much on
mionepaolo.lead: Three more death registers were opened, and the third of them gave up something the first two had hidden in plain sight. **From 1813 the volumes end with a «Tavola Alfabetica»** — a ruled table listing every death of the year by surname, with the village, the date, the act number and the folio. It turns a volume of faded handwriting into a single page that can be scanned in one look. The 1813 table carries seventeen names and not one of them is ours. The 1815 table carries twenty-two, and the second row reads **«De Franceschi Anna — Mione — 11 9bre»**.

act.when: **Saturday 11 November 1815**, Mione. **Matteo Lupieri**, Officer of the Civil State, went to the house on being notified. The act gives the death as *«jeri»* — the day before — at two in the morning
act.who: **«il Cadavere di Anna de Franceschi … in età d'anni quarantaquattro»** — forty-four years old, so **born about 1771**
act.child: **«nel Villaggio di Mione in casa di de Franceschi Paolo»** — the house is named by its head, and the head is a **Paolo de Franceschi** this archive did not have
act.brought: **«maritata col suddetto Paolo de Franceschi»** — married to that same Paolo. She carries the surname on the page, and so does her husband
act.witnesses: **«è nata in quell'istesso Villaggio di Mione»** — born in that same village, on the witnesses' own knowledge. The witnesses are **Fabris Osvaldo di Giuseppe** and **Fabris Giuseppe**, forty-four, tailor, both of Mione and no relation
act.signed: Matteo Lupieri, Officer of the Civil State
act.ref: Archivio di Stato di Udine · Stato civile napoleonico · Mione · Morti · 1815 · act **N. 23, folio 5** · Antenati ark an_ua667562, image 12 of 13; the alphabetical table is image 13

why.lab: A birth in about 1771 — a generation deeper than any register here reaches
why.text:
Civil registration at Mione begins in **1806**, and the death series begins in **November 1806**. Everything this page has built on the Mione family sits inside ten years of paper.

Anna's age puts her birth at **about 1771**, and the act says she was born **at Mione**. That is thirty-five years before the earliest surviving civil register, and it is the reason the death books were opened at all: *a death act states an age, and an age back-dates a birth.*

Her baptism can only be in the **Pieve di Gorto** books at Luincis. She is now the fourth named person this archive is waiting on that one collection for.

why.lab: Either the family married itself twice, or the clerk used her husband's name
why.text:
The page gives her as **«Anna de Franceschi»**, married to **«Paolo de Franceschi»**. There are two honest readings and this archive is not going to pick one without a second document.

**The first** is that she was born a de Franceschi. That is not a strange thing to propose here: the 1808 death act says in as many words that Antonio de Franceschi's wife was **«Giovanna, pure de Franceschi»** — *also* a de Franceschi — and the registrar wrote *pure* precisely so nobody would read it as a slip of the pen. Two De Franceschi couples in seven years, in a village of a few dozen houses, is what endogamy looks like.

**The second** is that Matteo Lupieri simply entered a married woman under her husband's surname. He does not do it elsewhere in this volume — the other women are given as *«nata»* somebody — which argues against it, but a single volume is thin evidence about a clerk's habits.

What is not in doubt is **Paolo**.

why.lab: Paolo is a fifth household
why.text:
The Mione De Franceschi households this archive can name now stand at five:

**Francesco the tailor**, husband of Margherita Gortan · **Osvaldo Antonio the carpenter**, husband of Cattarina Brencis — *and the 1809 death register says those two are brothers* · **Antonio the tailor**, husband of Giovanna «pure de Franceschi» · **Gio: Pietro Erman de Franceschi**, the fifty-five-year-old widower of 1808 who remarries Orsola in 1809 · and now **Paolo**, whose wife dies in his house in November 1815.

Paolo appears nowhere in the 1806–1812 births, marriages or deaths already read. He is a new name, and at a guess an older man — his wife was forty-four.

why.lab: What the tables cost, and what they save
why.text:
This is a method note, and it is worth writing down because it changes what is affordable.

Reading a Mione register act by act at a magnification where the hand is legible takes **three or four screen-fulls per page**, and the volumes run eleven to fifteen pages. The 1813 volume took seventeen passes to establish a **negative**.

The **Tavola Alfabetica** at the back of each volume from 1813 answers the same question in **three**. The 1815 table gave the surname, the village, the day, the month, the act number *and the folio* — enough to open the right leaf first time.

**1812 and earlier have no table.** Those still have to be read the slow way, and 1812 is half-read.

why.lab: 1813, read and clean
why.text:
For the record, since a negative result is a result: the **1813 death register** (ark an_ua667560, eleven images, acts on the rectos only) was read through, and then its alphabetical table was read as a check on the reading.

Seventeen deaths in the comune that year, across **Mione, Muina, Luint, Luincis, Ovasta, Agrons, Liariis and Entrampo**. The surnames are Bulfon, Della Pietra, Senni, Pol, Rossi, Raffael, Tolson, Steffani, Nino, Fortin, Duminj, Urban, Vernier and one *«infante maschio non battezzato»* at Agrons.

**No De Franceschi, in any role** — not as the dead, not as a parent, not as a witness. One near miss that cost two screenfuls: the witness at act 14 is an **«Osvald'Antonio»**, which is exactly our carpenter's name, and he turned out to be a **Tolson**.

mionemuina1814.heading: «Osvaldo de Franceschi», signed twice at Muina in 1814
mionemuina1814.grade: doc for both acts, for the age and for the fact that he signed · **inf, and openly contested, for the identification with the carpenter of Mione**
mionemuina1814.lead: The 1814 death register has **no alphabetical table** — those begin in 1813 and 1814 skipped one — so it had to be swept leaf by leaf. The surname appears on two of the eleven images, and on both it is not the registrar writing a name for an illiterate witness. It is **a signature, in a large confident upright hand**, twice.

act.when: **Act N. 12 — «Agenzia Comunale di Mione, li 10 dieci Settembre» 1814.** The registrar goes to **Muina** and views **Spinotti Candido**, born at Muina, son of *Giuseppe detto Candido Spinotti* and *Giovanna nata Paoletti*
act.who: **Act N. 13 — «Agenzia Comunale di Mione, li 26 ventisei Novembre dell'anno mille ottocento quattordici, giorno di Sabbato».** Again **«di Muina, frazione di quest'Agenzia»**, and again the same two men come to identify the body
act.child: **«Testimonj alla ricognizione furono Osvaldo de Franceschi d'anni 27 ventisette, Servitore»** — twenty-seven years old, and **a servant**
act.brought: With him both times: **Fabris Giovanni, forty-one, «pur Servitore»** — also a servant. The pair are described as **«non parenti, ma vicini del Defunto»** — no relation, but **neighbours**
act.witnesses: **«Osvaldo de Franceschi»**, written out in full, in a hand plainly not the clerk's — large, upright, an open looped capital O and a two-loop capital F. The same signature stands at the foot of both acts
act.signed: Valentino Lupieri, Officer of the Civil State, delegate. Act 12 carries a later visa in the margin: *«Palazzo li 6 9bre 1814»*
act.ref: Archivio di Stato di Udine · Stato civile napoleonico · Mione · Morti · 1814 · acts **N. 12 and N. 13** · Antenati ark an_ua667561, images 8 and 9 of 11

why.lab: Four ages against one, and the outlier loses
why.text:
This archive has been carrying an argument about when Osvaldo was born, because the registers disagree with themselves. The count now stands like this:

**October 1806** — about nineteen · **14 January 1809** — twenty-two · **August 1809** — twenty-two · **1810** — twenty-six · **10 September and 26 November 1814** — **twenty-seven**

Twenty-seven in late 1814 means born **1786 or 1787**, which is what the 1806 and both 1809 readings say. The 1810 act, which would put him at 1784, is now **four documents against one** and can be set aside as a clerk's estimate.

That is worth more than it looks. An ancestor with a birth year pinned to a two-year window is a person a parish book can be searched for; an ancestor with a five-year window is not.

why.lab: But a servant, and at Muina — so is this the same man?
why.text:
This is the part this archive will not smooth over, because smoothing it over is exactly the mistake that had to be retracted from the DNA page this month.

**In January 1809 Osvaldo Antonio de Franceschi is «falegname» — a carpenter — and «di Mione».** In September and November 1814 Osvaldo de Franceschi is **«Servitore»** — a servant — and a **neighbour** of two dead people at **Muina**.

**For one man:** the ages line up exactly (22 in January 1809 → 27 in autumn 1814); Mione and Muina are **seven hundred and eighty-four metres apart** across the Degano, which is not a migration, it is a walk; and the surname is not common enough in this comune for two men of the same forename to be casually assumed.

**For two men:** the trade is different and the place is different, and *«vicini del Defunto»* reads as a man who lives at Muina, not one who happened to be there. Muina is also where this archive's other Carnian strand sits — so a second Osvaldo there is not an idle possibility, it is the possibility that would matter most.

**Unresolved.** The 1814 acts are recorded here under both readings, and the Mione household table is not being rewritten on the strength of them.

why.lab: The one test that could settle it — and how far it gets
why.text:
Osvaldo signs his own name. So does the Osvaldo of 1809. **The two signatures can be laid side by side**, and they have been: *an_ua667556 image 3* against *an_ua667561 images 8 and 9*.

To my eye they are the same hand — the same oversized open **O**, the same *-ald-* ligature, the same double-looped capital **F**, the same absence of slant. The 1809 signature adds **«Ant.o»** and capitalises **«De»**; the 1814 one does neither.

**I am not a document examiner and this is not a finding.** It is a reason to lean one way, offered with the image references so that anyone who knows more than I do can look at the same two lines and disagree. What it is *not* is permission to merge the two men in the tables.

why.lab: What the rest of 1814 is worth
why.text:
A negative result is only as good as the method that produced it, so: **the 1813 negative is strong and the 1814 negative is weaker.**

1813 was read act by act *and* checked against the volume's own alphabetical table. 1814 has no table. It was swept page by page at a magnification that shows signature blocks clearly but not every name inside every act, and read closely only where the surname surfaced.

So the honest statement is: **the surname appears on images 8 and 9 of the 1814 volume, and a page-level sweep found it nowhere else.** If a De Franceschi is buried inside the body of one of the other acts as a parent, this pass could have missed them.

mionepaolo1812.heading: Two De Franceschi men sign the same page, 18 August 1812
mionepaolo1812.grade: doc — Mione, Morti 1812, read at high magnification 14 September 2026. The age discrepancy of one year is noted and not smoothed away
mionepaolo1812.lead: The 1812 death register has no alphabetical table either, so it was swept leaf by leaf. The surname appears once — and when it appears it appears **twice in the same act**, on the same line, and both men write their own names at the foot of it.

act.when: **Monday 18 August 1812, at eight in the morning**, Comune di Mione. **Matteo Lupieri**, Officer of the Civil State
act.who: **«il Cadavere di Ottaviani Valentino»** — died the previous day at five in the morning, aged **twenty-five**, by trade **«Sartore»**, a tailor, of Mione. Not of this family
act.child: **«Presenti alla ricognizione furono Erman de' Franceschi Gio: Pietro d'anni cinquantanove, Possidente»** — fifty-nine, and **a landowner**
act.brought: **«e de' Franceschi Paolo d'anni quarantadue»** — **forty-two**, so born about **1770**. Both domiciled at Mione
act.witnesses: Both sign. The block reads **«Erman de' Franceschi Gio: Pietro»** and, under it in a smaller, less practised hand, **«paolo de Franceschi»** — with a lower-case p
act.signed: Matteo Lupieri, Officer of the Civil State
act.ref: Archivio di Stato di Udine · Stato civile napoleonico · Mione · Morti · 1812 · Antenati ark an_ua667559, image 8 of 15

why.lab: Paolo, three years before his wife's funeral
why.text:
Paolo de Franceschi entered this archive an hour ago as **a house**: the address in the 1815 act where Anna died, *«in casa di de Franceschi Paolo»*. Here he is himself, alive, three years earlier, standing in a neighbour's house and signing his name.

**Forty-two in August 1812 means born about 1770.** Anna was **forty-four in November 1815**, so born about **1771**. Husband and wife born within a year of each other, both at Mione, both — on the face of the register — carrying the same surname.

He is the fifth Mione household and he is no longer only a doorway.

why.lab: And the Erman man, four years on and a class up
why.text:
**Gio: Pietro Erman de Franceschi** is already the best-documented adult male of the surname in this valley, and this is his fourth appearance:

**April 1808** — witness at a child's death, *«d'anni cinquantacinque in circa»*, **agricoltore** · **21 August 1808** — brings a newborn to the office, **fifty-eight**, **agricoltore** · **13 February 1809** — bridegroom, **fifty-six**, **agricoltore**, widower of Cattarina Carlevaris, marrying **Orsola de Franceschi**; born **28 April 1752** · **9 July 1809** — witness at a Muina birth, **fifty-four circa**, and already **«possidente»** · **August 1812** — witness here, **fifty-nine**, **«Possidente»**

**The trade changes, and the birth registers date the change much more tightly than the death register could.** Through 1808 and into February 1809 he works the land. **By 9 July 1809 — five months after the wedding — the register calls him a landowner**, and he is one still in 1812.

A man of fifty-six who marries a woman of forty and is styled *possidente* within half a year has, on the ordinary reading, **married property**. *Ordinary reading, not proof: a man can buy land in five months, and the word may simply be a different clerk's habit.*

*The one thing that does not fit is arithmetic.* Born 28 April 1752, he was **sixty** on 18 August 1812, and the act says fifty-nine. A year's slack in a register age is unremarkable — the earlier acts are just as loose — but it is recorded here rather than quietly rounded.

why.lab: «Erman de' Franceschi» is how the family writes itself
why.text:
This matters beyond one act. The 1679 list of village headmen names **«Zuane De Franceschi con un suo fiolo, Zuane d'Erman»** — and this archive has spent months treating *De Franceschi* and *Erman* as **two families** who happened to travel to Istria together.

In 1809 and again in 1812, a man signs himself **«Erman de' Franceschi»** — byname first, surname second, in his own hand, twice, four years apart. That is not a clerk's compound. **It is what the man called himself.**

So *Erman* at Mione is a **branch-name inside the surname**, not a separate surname — which changes how the 1679 line should be read, and it means every «Erman» entry in the Mione indexes is a candidate for this family rather than a neighbour's.

why.lab: What the 1812 volume is worth as a negative
why.text:
Fifteen images, no alphabetical table, swept page by page at a magnification that shows signature blocks clearly. **The surname appears on image 8 and nowhere else.**

The other signatures in the volume are Colledan, Fabris, Nino, Steffani, Pol, Gortan, Coluss, Sudretto and Ottaviani. As with 1814, a De Franceschi buried inside the body of another act as a parent could have escaped this pass. The 1813 and 1815 negatives, which have tables behind them, are stronger.

mionebanns.heading: Paolo has a son — and a series nobody had opened
mionebanns.grade: doc — Mione, «Pubblicazioni di matrimonio» 1815, read at high magnification 15 September 2026. The bride's mother's surname is not legible at any magnification this reading could reach
mionebanns.lead: Hunting for the birth registers, I mis-identified a run of nine volumes and opened one of them by accident. It is not a birth register. It is the **«pubblicazioni di matrimonio»** — the banns, read aloud in the square and nailed to the door of the town hall — and **a Napoleonic banns notice names the parents of both parties**. There is one such volume for every year from 1806 to 1815, and this archive had never opened a page of any of them.

act.when: **Sunday 4 June 1815, at ten in the morning**, Agenzia Comunale di Mione. **Matteo Lupieri**, Officer of the Civil State, reads the promise *«ad alta voce»* and has it **posted on the doors of the town hall** at the same hour
act.who: **«de' Franceschi Felice Santo, di professione Sartore, nativo e domiciliato nella Frazione di Mione»** — a **tailor**, born and living at Mione
act.child: **«figlio di de' Franceschi Paolo e di Anna nata Brunis giugali»** — son of **Paolo de Franceschi** and **Anna née Brunis**, married
act.brought: The bride: **«de' Canova Lucia Santa, figlia del fu Osvaldo Antonio e Lucia nata Pellia…»**, *possidente*, **born and living at Liariis, agenzia d'Ovaro**
act.witnesses: This is the **second** publication — *«prosseguendo ad altra una volta la promessa di Matrimonio»*. The first stands earlier in the same volume
act.signed: Matteo Lupieri, Officer of the Civil State
act.ref: Archivio di Stato di Udine · Stato civile napoleonico · Mione · **Pubblicazioni di matrimonio** · 1815 · Antenati ark **an_ua667552**, image 6 of 7

why.lab: Anna was not born a de Franceschi — and that corrects me
why.text:
Yesterday this page set out two readings of the 1815 death act and refused to choose between them. The act called the dead woman **«Anna de Franceschi»** and her husband **«Paolo de Franceschi»**, and I wrote that either she was born to the surname — which the 1808 *«Giovanna **pure** de Franceschi»* shows is possible here — or the clerk had entered a wife under her husband's name.

**Five months before she died, the banns name her «Anna nata Brunis».** She married into the surname. **The second reading was right and I should say so plainly.**

The reasoning that pointed the other way was not wrong, only outweighed: the 1808 act really does go out of its way to write *pure*, and that couple really were both De Franceschi. One endogamous marriage at Mione, not two.

*On the surname itself:* the hand gives **Brunis**. **Brencis** — a family already documented in this village, and the surname of Osvaldo the carpenter's wife — cannot be excluded at this resolution, and the marriage allegati would settle it.

why.lab: A sixth man, and the fourth tailor
why.text:
**Felice Santo de' Franceschi** is new. He is Paolo's son, he is a **sartore**, and in June 1815 he is old enough to marry.

The trade keeps returning. **Francesco** is a tailor (1806–1810). **Antonio** is a tailor (1808). The young man whose body Paolo and Gio: Pietro identify in **1812** is a tailor. And now **Felice Santo**. In a comune whose other men are *agricoltori*, *falegnami* and *possidenti*, the De Franceschi of Mione are **needleworkers, repeatedly** — and the tailor is the **cramar** trade this archive has argued walked over the mountains into Istria.

His mother dies **five months after these banns**, aged forty-four.

why.lab: The marriage itself is almost certainly at Ovaro, not here
why.text:
The bride is **of Liariis, in the agenzia d'Ovaro**. Under the Napoleonic code the banns are published in **both** communes and the marriage is celebrated in **the bride's**.

The Mione *Matrimoni* volume for 1815 runs to five images and does not contain this marriage. **The act should be in Ovaro's 1815 marriage register** — a body this archive has never read, although it has read all twenty-six volumes of Ovaro's *allegati*.

That also means **the allegati for this marriage are Ovaro's**, and allegati carry baptismal extracts. Felice Santo's extract would come out of the **Pieve di Gorto** books and would give **Paolo and Anna's own generation a date**.

why.lab: Nine volumes, none of them read
why.text:
The banns series for Mione runs **1806, 1808, 1809, 1810, 1811, 1812, 1813, 1814, 1815** — Antenati arks **an_ua667544 to an_ua667552** — between fifty and sixty images in all.

They are worth more per page than the marriage registers, because a banns notice does in four lines what a marriage act does in two pages: **it names both parties, their trades, their villages, and the names of all four parents**, with *«del fu»* marking which of them were already dead.

This was found by mistake, while looking for the birth registers — which are still not located.

why.lab: Batta and Maria are below the floor of every register here
why.text:
Civil registration at Mione starts in **1806**. Everything this page has built on the Mione family stands on ten years of paper, and the one earlier fixed point is the **1679** headmen's list — a gap of a hundred and twenty-seven years with three names in it.

**Batta de' Franceschi and Maria née Brenis put a married couple into that gap.** Their daughter Ottavia was old enough to bear a son in about **1780**, so Ottavia was born around **1750–1760**, and her parents married before that — **born, most likely, in the 1720s or 1730s**.

They are **dead by August 1812** and they appear in **no other act** of the Mione civil registers: not as parents in the births, not in the marriages, not in the deaths 1806–1815, all of which have now been read. **The only reason this archive has them at all is that a Napoleonic clerk had to say whose daughter the groom's mother was.**

They are the deepest named De Franceschi couple this project holds from Carnia outside the 1679 list.

why.lab: A married-out daughter, and a name for the pattern
why.text:
Ottavia married a **Zanelli** of **Ovasta** and vanished into that surname — which is precisely the disappearance this archive has been tracking under the heading of the married-out daughters. She is only visible because **her son's banns had to name her**.

The list already holds Giacoma marrying a merchant of Chialina in 1806, the Muina bride of 1808, and Orsola marrying **Erman de Franceschi** in 1809. **Ottavia is a generation older than all three** and comes from the other direction: not from a marriage act, but from a *grandchild's*.

**That is the method, stated:** where a daughter's own marriage is missing, her children's banns will name her — with her maiden surname and her father's.

why.lab: Brenis, twice, and what it does for Anna
why.text:
Yesterday's correction rested on a single word read once: Paolo's wife **«Anna nata Brunis»** in the 1815 banns.

Here the same surname stands again, three years earlier and in the same register series, as **«Maria nata Brenis»**. Two women of that name marry De Franceschi men a generation apart.

**And the family is already in these books under a third spelling**: the entire 1806 death register of Mione consists of **one act**, for a **Brenci** child. Osvaldo the carpenter's wife is **Cattarina Brencis**; the second witness at the 1808 child's death is **Agostino Brencis**.

**Brenci · Brencis · Brenis · Brunis** — and the 1808 birth register adds **Prencis**, with an unmistakable capital **P**.

*I first wrote this as «one Mione family, four spellings». That is firmer than the evidence allows, and it is loosened here rather than left standing:* **B** and **P** are not letters this hand confuses, so *Prencis/Brencis* — the carpenter's wife — and *Brenis/Brunis* — Ottavia's mother and Paolo's wife — are **two clusters that may join, not one settled name**.

The correction to Anna does not depend on it: what that turned on was *«nata»* followed by a surname of any spelling.

why.lab: And the marriage act should be here, not at Ovaro
why.text:
Unlike the 1815 banns, **this one does not send the act away.** Both parties live at **Ovasta**, which is a frazione of the Comune di Mione, so the marriage itself belongs to **Mione's own Matrimoni register for 1812** — ark an_ua667521, eleven images, **not yet read**.

That act would give Giambattista Zanelli's age again, name all four parents again, and — if it follows the pattern of the 1809 marriage — carry **allegati**: baptismal extracts copied out of the **Pieve di Gorto** books, which is the only place Batta and Maria can be found alive.

why.lab: Yesterday's open question now has an answer, and it is the other man
why.text:
Yesterday this page published two acts of **1814** in which an **«Osvaldo de Franceschi d'anni ventisette, Servitore»** identifies the dead at **Muina** and signs his own name. I set out two readings — the carpenter of Mione, or a second Osvaldo at Muina — refused to merge anything, and wrote that *«a second Osvaldo there is not an idle possibility, it is the possibility that would matter most.»*

**This archive already held that second Osvaldo and I did not put him in the frame.** He is **Osvaldo de Franceschi of Muina, born 14 March 1788**, son of **Antonio q.m Leonardo** and **Maria née Corva**, who married Appolonia Galante on 28 January 1808 and whose daughter Anna Maria was born at Muina in December 1809.

Three things now point at him rather than at the carpenter:

**The village.** The 1814 witnesses are *«vicini del Defunto»* — neighbours — at **Muina**. The Muina Osvaldo lives at Muina. The carpenter is *«di Mione»* in every act that names him.

**The trade.** *Agricoltore* to *servitore* is a small step; *falegname* to *servitore* is not.

**And the arithmetic, which is the part that convinced me.** Born 14 March 1788, he was **nineteen years and ten months** on 17 January 1808 and the banns call him **twenty**. He was **twenty-six and a half** on 10 September 1814 and **twenty-six and eight months** on 26 November, and both acts call him **twenty-seven**. *The same rounding, six years apart, producing the recorded figure exactly both times.*

why.lab: And the signature comparison should be withdrawn
why.text:
Yesterday I laid the 1809 signature of the Mione carpenter beside the 1814 signatures at Muina and wrote that to my eye they were the same hand — the same oversized **O**, the same *-ald-* ligature, the same double-looped **F** — while saying plainly that I am not a document examiner and that it was *«a reason to lean one way»*, not a finding.

**The lean was in the wrong direction, and I should retire the observation rather than defend it.** If the 1814 man is the Muina Osvaldo, then what I was looking at is two men who learned to write in the same valley from the same kind of teacher — which is exactly what period handwriting looks like, and exactly the trap I flagged and walked into anyway.

The hedge did its job. The observation did not.

why.lab: Galante, a fifth and sixth time, in a clear looped G
why.text:
The bride's surname is written **Galante** twice on this leaf — once in the act and once in the *Avviso* — in the same clear looped capital the notary used.

This archive published **Salante**, corrected it to **Galante** on the strength of four hands against two, and renamed sixteen occurrences. The count is now **six against two**, from a document that was not part of the original argument.

The two dissenters remain what they were: the **parish priest** writing the baptismal extract, and the **clerk who docketed the file**. Both were copying from the baptismal book, so *Salante* is what stands in the **Pieve di Gorto** register — which is worth knowing when that book is finally read.

why.lab: What a banns notice does that a marriage act cannot
why.text:
Two things, and both are visible here.

**It states the wedding before it happens.** *«Il matrimonio sarà celebrato li vent'otto Gennajo corrente nel Villaggio di Muina»* — eleven days ahead, with the village named. Where a marriage act is missing or filed in another comune, the banns still say when and where to look.

**And it gives an age on a fixed day.** Ages in these registers drift; an age attached to a stated Sunday, checked against a baptismal date the allegati already supply, turns the drift into a **measurable habit** — which is what let this page tell two Osvaldos apart.

Appolonia is given as *«d'anni venticinque e mezzo»* — twenty-five **and a half**, an oddly exact figure for a clerk. Born 3 May 1782, she was twenty-five years and eight months. He was rounding *down* for her and *up* for the groom, on the same line.

close.text:
**Ninety-one images for four notices** is a poor hit rate by volume and an excellent one by content, because of what a banns notice contains that a marriage act does not.

It gave this archive **a son for Paolo**, **a maiden name for Anna** that overturned a published reading, **a married-out daughter** nobody had, **her parents** — a couple born in the 1720s or 1730s who appear in no other act — and **an age on a stated Sunday** that told two Osvaldos apart.

That is five things the Mione births, marriages and deaths, all read, could not supply.

close.lab: And what the negatives are worth, honestly
close.text:
Five of the nine volumes returned nothing. Those were read **page by page at a magnification that shows a name of that length clearly** — the method that found the 1812 notice on a first pass.

But it is a sweep, not a transcription. **A De Franceschi buried mid-sentence as a grandparent, in a faint hand, could have escaped it.** The 1813 negative is the strongest of the five because the volume's own alphabetical table confirms it independently; the other four rest on the sweep alone.

Recorded that way rather than as nine clean volumes.

why.lab: The series is called «Pubblicazioni ed opposizioni»
why.text:
The title leaf of the 1806 volume gives the series its full name: ***«Registro per l'esposizione delle pubblicazioni matrimoniali, e per le opposizioni»*** — **publications, and oppositions**.

A banns notice is not a record of a marriage. **It is a notice inviting the world to object**, posted where the government's orders are posted, and read aloud twice on successive Sundays precisely so that anyone with an impediment has time to say so. Most of them are followed by a wedding. **Some are not**, and the register was designed with that in mind.

So the honest reading of the August 1812 notices is: *a marriage was promised, announced twice, and does not appear in the register of the comune it belonged to, that year or in the two years after.* Whether it was stopped, delayed beyond this archive's reach, or celebrated somewhere I have not looked, this page does not know.

why.lab: What it does not touch
why.text:
**The Ottavia finding is unaffected.** She and her parents are named in the notices themselves, which were read aloud and posted by a public official who had to get the filiation right — that is the whole point of the document.

**Batta de Franceschi and Maria née Brenis stand.** So does Ottavia's marriage to Francesco Zanelli, who is alive in 1812 and named as such. What is in doubt is only whether *their son* married Lucia Roder that autumn.

why.lab: And how much the negative is worth
why.text:
Less than it looks, and that is worth saying.

Three of the volume's six acts were read closely; **three were swept at page level only**, at a magnification that shows surnames in signature blocks and marginal notes but not every name inside a paragraph.

The 1813 and 1814 checks are stronger, because both volumes carry their own **alphabetical tables** listing every marriage of the year by surname — but the 1814 table's left column is partly lost in the binding shadow, and I read it in a crop that clipped the first letters of two rows.

**So: probably not married at Mione in 1812–14, and not certainly.** The next thing to read is the three untranscribed acts.

mionemargherita.heading: «Suo fratello Osvaldo» — a sister nobody had, and a child nobody had
mionemargherita.grade: doc — Mione, Nati 1808, act N. 16, read at high magnification 15 September 2026
mionemargherita.lead: The Mione **birth** registers were finally located — they are not where I first looked, and they stop in 1810 — and the 1808 volume was opened. Act sixteen is four lines long and it does two things at once: **it names a child this archive did not have, and it names a sister.**

act.when: **Sunday 10 July 1808**, Comune di Mione. The registrar **Valentino Lupieri**
act.who: **«Si è presentata … de' Franceschi Margherita, dell'età d'anni ventidue, domiciliata nel villaggio di Mione, villica di professione, portando seco un Infante di sesso femmineo»** — a woman of **twenty-two**, carrying a baby into the office herself

act.signed: **«Notificante de' Franceschi Margherita per non saper scrivere fa la croce ✝»**

why.lab: A fourth sibling, and this one is documented rather than argued
why.text:
This archive has been building a sibling group out of inference. The 1809 death register calls **Francesco and Osvaldo** *«fratelli de Franceschi»* in as many words — that part was always documented. **Giacoma** was added to them by argument: she is *«q.m Osualdo»*, and so are they, probably.

**Margherita needs no argument.** She stands in front of the registrar and says the child is her brother's. *«Suo fratello Osvaldo de' Franceschi, di professione Fallegname»* — the trade matches the carpenter exactly, the village matches, and the wife's name matches.

**Twenty-two in July 1808 means born about 1786** — between Francesco (about 1784–85) and Osvaldo (about 1786–87), which is where a sister belongs. The group is now **Francesco, Osvaldo Antonio, Margherita** documented, and **Giacoma** still inferred.

why.lab: And a granddaughter for the dead Osvaldo
why.text:
**Cattarina de' Franceschi, born 10 July 1808 at eight in the morning**, is new. The carpenter's household had one known child — Giovanni Battista, born 15 October 1810 — and now it has an elder daughter.

She is also the earliest-born child in the Mione household table with **an hour** attached to her, and she was registered **the same day she was born**, which is unusual in this register: most acts come a day or two late.

why.lab: She could not write, and that is now a pattern with four points
why.text:
*«per non saper scrivere fa la croce»* — she made her mark.

Six months later her brothers **Francesco and Osvaldo both sign their own names** at the foot of a death act. Three years before, their kinswoman **Giacoma** signed hers — *«Giacoma de Franceschi q.m Osualdo affermo m.p.»*, manu propria, at eighteen. And in February 1809 **Orsola**, aged forty, could not sign her marriage and her husband signed for her.

So the line is not simply drawn by sex after all: **Giacoma could write and Margherita could not**, and they are the same generation in the same village. This archive has said twice that literacy here is *«drawn by sex, not by generation»*. **On four data points that is too neat**, and the honest statement is that it varied household by household.

why.lab: Prencis, with a P — and a surname that will not hold still
why.text:
The wife's surname here is written **Prencis**, with an unmistakable capital **P**. *This page first said the 1810 act writes her **Brencis**; reading that act directly gives **Crencis**, and the capital is neither of the other two.*

Yesterday, on the strength of *Brenci* (1806), *Brencis* (1808 and 1810), *Brenis* (1812) and *Brunis* (1815), I wrote that these were *«one Mione family, four spellings in ten years of the same clerks' handwriting»*.

**With a clear P in front of one of them, that is firmer than the evidence allows.** *B* and *P* are not letters this hand confuses. It may still be one family — Friulian surnames drift hard — but **Prencis/Brencis** (the carpenter's wife) and **Brenis/Brunis** (Ottavia's mother, and Paolo's wife) should be treated as two clusters that *may* join, not as one settled name. The Anna correction does not depend on it: what that turned on was *«nata»* plus a surname of any spelling.

why.lab: Where the births stop
why.text:
The Mione **Nati** on Antenati are **1806, 1808, 1809 and 1810** — arks an_ua667570 to an_ua667573 — and then nothing. The ark space above 667573 is empty, checked twice.

The other series run to **1815**: marriages, marriage allegati, banns and deaths all do. **Only the births stop, and they stop in 1810.**

So **Giovanni Battista, born 15 October 1810, is the last De Franceschi birth the civil registers of this comune can give this archive.** Any child born to Francesco and Margherita Gortan, to Osvaldo and Cattarina, or to Paolo and Anna between 1811 and 1815 is invisible here — and can only be in the **Pieve di Gorto**.

why.lab: Whose child is it?
why.text:
The act does not say — which is exactly what makes act 16 six pages earlier so valuable, because that one *did*: *«suo fratello Osvaldo»*.

What can be said: a man of fifty-six does not carry a stranger's newborn to the town hall. And **Gio: Pietro Erman de Franceschi is the son of a dead Pietro Erman** — so a living **Pietro Ermanni** at Mione in 1808, married and with a first child, is most naturally **his own son, named for his grandfather**. The alternative is a brother.

**Inferred, and labelled so.** What is documented is the household itself: **Pietro Ermanni × Orsola née Crosilla**, agricoltori of Mione, and their son **Gio: Batta Benedetto, born 20 August 1808 at three in the afternoon**.

One more detail worth keeping: the father is entered as plain **«Ermanni»** while the older man signs **«Erman De Franceschi»**. The compound name is the elder's; the son is written short.

why.lab: And here is where I have to mark my own argument down
why.text:
Yesterday I settled which Osvaldo stood at Muina in 1814 partly on **age arithmetic** — the Muina man's recorded ages rounding the same way in 1808 and 1814 — and I called that *«the part that convinced me»*.

**Set Gio: Pietro's recorded ages beside his documented birth of 28 April 1752 and the method looks weaker:**

**April 1808** — *«cinquantacinque in circa»*, when he was 55 turning 56 · **21 August 1808** — **fifty-eight**, when he was 56 · **13 February 1809** — fifty-six, when he was 56 · **9 July 1809** — ***«cinquantaquattro circa»***, when he was **57** · **August 1812** — fifty-nine, when he was 60

A spread of **fifty-four to fifty-nine** for a man who was fifty-six to sixty — in the same commune, in the same registers, sometimes months apart. **Four months after being called fifty-five he is called fifty-eight; eleven months after that, fifty-four.**

The Osvaldo identification does not fall — it rested on the **village** and the **trade** as much as the age, and those still point one way. But the age leg of it is now worth less than I said, and saying so is cheaper than being caught by it later.

why.lab: A doctor at Luint
why.text:
**«Lupieri Gio: Batta, d'anni trentadue, medico di professione»** — a thirty-two-year-old physician, standing as a witness at a farm birth.

The Lupieri run through every act of this comune: **Valentino Lupieri** is the registrar and a witness by turns, **Matteo Lupieri** succeeds him, another Lupieri is thirty and attinato. This one is a doctor, and he is at Luint — the village whose men also show up at Mione weddings as tailors.

It is a small correction to the picture of an isolated alpine commune. **There was a physician a mile up the valley in 1808**, and he could write.

mionematteo.heading: Matteo the shoemaker, and a daughter who was «illetterata»
mionematteo.grade: doc — Mione, Nati 1809, act N. 4, read at high magnification 15 September 2026
mionematteo.lead: The 1809 birth register opens a household this archive did not have, headed by a man carrying **the deepest name in the whole Mione file**. It also puts one blunt Latin-derived word on the page that the archive should not soften.

act.when: **Thursday 2 March 1809**, Comune di Mione. Registrar **Valentino Lupieri**
act.who: **«Si è presentato al sottoscritto Ufficiale dello Stato Civile Maria figlia di Matteo de Franceschi, d'anni dieci otto circa, domiciliata nel Villaggio di Mione, villica di condizione, portando seco un Infante di sesso femminile»** — a girl of about **eighteen**, carrying the baby herself
act.child: Born **that same day at two in the morning** at Mione, and given two names: **Giovanna-Maddalena**
act.brought: **«La suddetta Maria de Franceschi ha pure dichiarato essere la neonata figlia di Matteo de Franceschi di professione Calzolajo, e di Anna nata Fasiol sua moglie»** — a **shoemaker** and his wife, both of Mione
act.witnesses: **Valentino Lupieri**, thirty-one, *possidente*, and **Gio: Battista Roter**, twenty-four, **also a Calzolajo**, both of Luint
act.signed: **«Notificante de Deffranceschi Maria illetterata fa il segno di croce ✝»**
act.ref: Archivio di Stato di Udine · Stato civile napoleonico · Mione · **Nati** · 1809 · act **N. 4** · Antenati ark **an_ua667572**, image 4 of 15

why.lab: There are two Matteos, and this is the younger
why.text:
**Matteo** has stood at the bottom of this family's Mione pedigree as a patronymic and nothing else: Orsola's baptismal extract of 1809 calls her *«figlia legittima e naturale di **Pietro quondam Matteo** De Franceschi di Mione»* — daughter of Pietro, son of the **late** Matteo. Orsola was born in 1768, so that Matteo belongs to a generation born around the **1710s** and was dead before 1809.

**This Matteo is alive in March 1809**, works as a **shoemaker**, has a daughter of eighteen and a newborn. He was born somewhere around **1765–75**.

**They are not the same man**, and this archive will not weld them. What it does show is the thing the burial ground at Gorto already suggested: *the names come round again.* An elder Matteo, a grandson or nephew given his name, two generations apart in one village of a few dozen houses.

And it is a **fifth trade** for the surname here — after the tailors, the carpenter, the farmers and the landowner, a *calzolajo*.

why.lab: «Illetterata» — the register's own word
why.text:
The registrar did not write *«per non saper scrivere»*, which is the ordinary formula and the one used for Margherita eight months earlier. He wrote **«de Deffranceschi Maria illetterata fa il segno di croce»**.

**Unlettered.** It is a harsher word and it is the clerk's, not this archive's, and it is quoted rather than paraphrased for that reason.

She was about eighteen, and she had walked her newborn sister to the town hall at an hour of the morning when the child was a few hours old. **Giacoma de Franceschi signed her own marriage at eighteen in 1806.** Maria could not sign a birth act at eighteen in 1809, in the same village. That is the second pair this week that breaks the neat rule, and the rule should stay broken.

why.lab: Two shoemakers and a landowner
why.text:
The witnesses are **Valentino Lupieri, thirty-one, possidente** — the registrar's own kinsman, here as a private man — and **Gio: Battista Roter, twenty-four, calzolajo**, *both of Luint*.

A shoemaker's child is witnessed by another shoemaker. The 1806 marriage of Giacoma was witnessed by **four tailors**. The 1808 birth of Cattarina was witnessed by a **Micoli-Toscano** of the palace family and a Lupieri.

**The witness lists are a trade directory.** They are also the part of these acts this archive read past for months while collecting parents, and they are where the village actually shows itself.

why.lab: And the count of births is wrong, in this archive's favour
why.text:
This page has said that the alphabetical index of births for 1806–1810 *«opens on three De Franceschi entries … Anna-Maria, Anna-Cecilia and Gio: Batta»*.

**Those were the first three lines, not the whole of it.** Two more are now read straight off the registers: **Cattarina**, 10 July 1808, and **Giovanna-Maddalena**, 2 March 1809. The true figure for De Franceschi births at Mione in those five years is **at least five**, and the birth index itself has not yet been located on Antenati — the three-page tables at arks an_ua667540 and an_ua667566 turn out to be the **marriage** and **death** indexes for the same span.

mionenati1810.heading: The last two births, and a man who signs his name two ways
mionenati1810.grade: doc for both acts · the wife's surname is **not** settled and this page stops pretending it is
mionenati1810.lead: The 1810 birth register is the last one the civil series has — the Mione **Nati** stop here while the marriages, banns and deaths run on to 1815. It holds two De Franceschi acts, and between them they close a household, open a question about a surname, and demolish an argument I made two days ago.

act.when: **Act N. 1 — Sunday 14 January 1810.** *«Si è presentato … **Francesco de' Franceschi, d'anni ventisei circa, di professione Sarto**, portando seco un infante di sesso feminile nato il giorno d'oggi **alle ore tre antimeridiane** … a cui furono imposti i nomi di **Anna Cecilia**»*
act.who: The child is *«sua figlia … dalla **Margherita nata Gortan** sua consorte»*. Witnesses **Antonio Bressan**, twenty-six, *domestico*, and **Matteo Lupieri**, *possidente*, of Luint. **Francesco signs his own name.** Anna Cecilia is dead at one month on 28 January
act.child: **Act N. 21 — Thursday 15 October 1810.** *«… **de Franceschi Osvaldo, d'anni ventisei**, di professione **fa legname**, portando seco un infante di sesso maschile nato il giorno d'oggi **alle ore dieci antimeridiane** … a cui fu imposto il nome di **Gio: Batta**»*
act.brought: *«essere il neonato suo figlio, e di **Cattarina nata Crencis** sua consorte, di professione **fa legname il primo, agricoltrice la seconda**»*
act.witnesses: **Roter Gio: Batta**, twenty-four, **calzolajo**, and **Brovedan Pietro**, twenty-seven, **sarto**, both of **Luint**
act.signed: **«de franceski osualdo»** — in his own hand, lower-case, rough
act.ref: Archivio di Stato di Udine · Stato civile napoleonico · Mione · **Nati** · 1810 · acts **N. 1 and N. 21** · Antenati ark **an_ua667573**, images 3 and 12 of 15

why.lab: The same man, twenty-one months apart, in two different hands
why.text:
In **January 1809** Osvaldo signs a death act **«Osvaldo Ant.o De Franceschi»** — upright, confident, capitals on both parts of the surname, the *Ant.o* abbreviated in the way a practised writer abbreviates.

In **October 1810** the same man signs his own son's birth **«de franceski osualdo»**. Lower-case throughout. Surname first. *Franceschi* spelled **franceski**. His own forename spelled **osualdo**.

**Two days ago I laid two signatures side by side and said they looked like one hand.** I hedged it — *«I am not a document examiner and this is not a finding»* — and then withdrew it a day later when the 1808 banns pointed at a different man.

**Here is the proof that the withdrawal was right, and it comes from the man himself.** One person, twenty-one months, two hands so different that if I had found them in separate parishes I would have called them separate people. **Signature comparison at this magnification, in this valley, in this century, is worth nothing**, and this page will not do it again.

why.lab: And the wife's surname is written differently every single time
why.text:
This archive has now read the same woman's maiden name in five registers, and got a different first letter in most of them:

**Brenci** — the single act of the 1806 death register · **Prencis** — the 1808 birth of her daughter Cattarina, a clear **P** · **Crencis** — this act, October 1810, and the capital is neither of the first two · **Brencis** — what this archive recorded from the 1810 act before I read it myself · **Brenis** — Ottavia's mother in the 1812 banns · **Brunis** — Paolo's wife Anna in the 1815 banns

*I have tried three times to decide what this surname is, and each attempt has been overtaken by the next act.* **The honest position is that the clerks of Mione could not spell it either**, and that **B, P and C are not distinguishable in this hand at the head of this word.**

So the name is recorded here as **«Brenci / Prencis / Crencis»** with the act each spelling comes from, and no preferred form. The two women — the carpenter's wife and Paolo's — may or may not be of one family; **the spelling cannot decide it, and neither can I.**

why.lab: Where the 1810 outlier came from
why.text:
The age of Osvaldo the carpenter has been argued on this page for days. He is about **nineteen** in October 1806, **twenty-two** in January 1809, **twenty-two** again in August 1809 — and **twenty-six** in one act of 1810, which the archive called an outlier and set aside.

**This is that act, read directly rather than at second hand: «de Franceschi Osvaldo, d'anni ventisei».** The outlier is real and it is his own son's birth, reported by him in person.

Which, set beside Gio: Pietro Erman being recorded 55, 58, 56, 54 and 59 across five acts for an actual 56 to 60, says the plain thing: **ages in these registers are worth about three years either way, even when the man himself is standing at the desk.**

why.lab: Luint again, and the trades again
why.text:
Both 1810 acts are witnessed by men of **Luint** — the next village — and both pairs are tradesmen: **Antonio Bressan** a *domestico* and **Matteo Lupieri** a *possidente* in January; **Roter Gio: Batta** a **shoemaker** and **Brovedan Pietro** a **tailor** in October.

**Roter the shoemaker is the same man who witnessed Matteo the shoemaker's child in March 1809**, aged twenty-four then and twenty-four now. A shoemaker stands for a shoemaker, a tailor for a tailor. These witness lists are the village's trade directory, and they are the part of a birth act this archive spent months reading past.

**And with Gio: Batta, 15 October 1810, the civil births stop.** Any child born to these households between 1811 and 1815 is in the **Pieve di Gorto** or nowhere.
